To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) DNNs generalize much better on controlled real-world noisy labels, (2) DNBs may not learn the patterns first on real-word noisy labels, and (3) robust learning methods that work on synthetic noise may or may not work on real-world noise.

(1): DNNs generalize much better on synthetic noise, but not on real-world noise (2): DNNs may learn different things on synthetic vs real-world noise (3): ImageNet architectures generalize better on synthetic noise than VGG architectures, but the reverse is true for real-world noise (4): Real-world noise may be less harmful, but it is more difficult to improve on (5): Robust learning methods for synthetic noise may not generalize well to real-world noise, or
(1) deep learning on real-world noisy labels is different from synthetic noise, and (2) deep learning on synthetic noise does not necessarily translate to real-world noisy labels.

understanding the difference between synthetic vs. real-world noise in the context of deep learning.
the question: how well do deep networks learn on real-world noise?

the following questions: (1) How do deep learning models generalize to different noise levels and types of noise? (2) What is the difference between synthetic and real-world noise? (3) How can we improve deep learning robustness on noisy data?

real-world noise is much more challenging than the commonly used synthetic noise.

(1), DNNs are more robust to real-world noise than synthetic noise; (2), DNNs do not learn patterns on real-world noisy labels; (3), ImageNet architectures can be fine-tuned to generalize well on noisy labels; (4), real-world noise may be less harmful but it is more difficult to improve; (5), methods that work well for synthetic noise may not perform as well on real noise, and vice-versa
DNNs are surprisingly robust to real-world noisy labels, and the gap between real-world and synthetic noise is much larger than we thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the performance of DNNs on real-world noise may not be a good proxy for their performance on synthetic noise, and that the performance of a method on one type of noise may not generalize to the other.
deep learning is more robust than expected on real-world noise.
the noise types, noise levels, and training settings all matter in deep learning research.
